Kennedy Space Center LC-39A, 2023-10-13. Psyche is NASA's first mission to a metal-rich M-class asteroid — a 226-km-diameter body believed to be the exposed nickel-iron core of a differentiated proto-planet. Insight into Psyche's interior is insight into the cores of every rocky planet, including Earth's.
Falcon Heavy second stage delivers Psyche to escape velocity. Ion thrusters take over within hours of separation — continuous low-thrust acceleration shapes the entire transfer.
Hall-effect ion thrusters (four SPT-140s, 4.5 kW each) commissioned. Continuous low-thrust acceleration over the next 4+ years gradually expands the heliocentric orbit toward Psyche.
2026-05-15. Closest approach 4,609 km. Added the orbital energy that ion thrust alone couldn't deliver in a reasonable time frame, accelerating Psyche outward to the main belt.
Mid-cruise trajectory refinement. Ion thrust continues.
Planned 2029-08. Psyche enters the asteroid's gravitational sphere of influence. Ion engines slow the spacecraft for gradual capture.

Ion-thrust gravitational capture into a high orbit (700 km altitude). Over the following 26-month mission, Psyche will descend through four orbit phases (A → B → C → D), mapping the asteroid's gravity, magnetism, topography, and composition. If the metal-core hypothesis is right, Psyche will look fundamentally unlike any other small body we've seen — exposed metal surface with iron-sulphide deposits, none of the rubble-pile chaos of typical asteroids.
First mission to a metal-rich M-class asteroid; first interplanetary spacecraft to use Hall-effect thrusters

Psyche reaches for the exposed nickel-iron core of a differentiated proto-planet — a 226-km metal body that may be the closest analogue to Earth's own core anywhere accessible. Launched 2023-10-13 on a Falcon Heavy from Kennedy LC-39A. Four SPT-140 Hall-effect ion thrusters spiral the trajectory outward; a Mars gravity assist in May 2026 (4,609 km closest approach) added the energy ion thrust alone couldn't deliver in time. Arrival planned 2029-08, followed by a 26-month four-orbit-phase descent (A → B → C → D) mapping the asteroid's gravity, magnetism, topography, and composition. If the metal-core hypothesis is right, Psyche will look unlike anything else we've visited — bare metal surface, iron-sulphide deposits, none of the rubble-pile chaos of typical asteroids.
Four Hall-effect ion thrusters take over. Continuous low-thrust acceleration over 4+ years.
2026-05-15. Closest approach 4,609 km — Mars flyby completed.
Ion-thrust gravitational capture into 700-km orbit. 26-month mission, four orbit phases.
